General.Description:
Between 1942 and 1945, Thomas Birchfield's father wrote 247 letters home from the Western Front. Thomas's mother kept every one of them, tied in batches with different-coloured ribbon — one colour for each year, one ribbon for each theatre of the war his father passed through. When Thomas's mother died in 2009, he found them in a box under her bed. He spent the next eight years reading them.

Letters from the Front is not a military history. It is the record of a son reconstructing a father he never knew — his father came home from the war a different man, one who did not speak about what had happened, and who died of a heart attack when Thomas was eleven — through the voice of a young man who still expected to come home unchanged.

Birchfield interweaves the letters themselves (which he quotes extensively) with his own reflections on reading them, and with the history he researched to understand the context of what his father was living through. The result is a memoir of extraordinary tenderness and genuine historical weight.

There is enormous love in these pages — the love in the letters themselves, and the love of a son for a father he only came to know through paper and ink, sixty years too late.

A deeply moving and important book.
